background.speaker: [target]
background.text: I think it's easy to believe that things are a meritocracy. It's what people aspire to be. It's how people talk about their companies. It's how people talk about their industries. But you start seeing like little things that don't really fit in and you try to explain it away. Well, that's just that one guy. Or, oh, that's just this one situation. Or maybe I should have been a little bit more aggressive here. And then you realize all of a sudden all these things are adding up and they don't make sense in the world that is a meritocracy. And you see it happening to other people who are all women or are all one type of person or not another type of person. And all of a sudden you realize, wow, this is not a meritocratic environment. And it doesn't matter how often they say it. I still see that I'm not invited to these things. And no woman is invited because they're women. That is not a meritocratic environment. And you start wondering why is it and how do I fix it?

background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: Well, so that's a really good point, and I'm sure that there are so many women in this room that feel these. I know that in the tech world, a lot of women call them the microaggressions. But I think if there's one thing I learned in making this documentary, this is not just in tech, right? This crosses all sorts of industry. These microaggressions, death by a thousand cuts, the thing that drive women from the workforce. So at what point did you realize that this wasn't something that you should just let roll off your back?

background.speaker: [target]
background.text: That's a good question. I think early on I would start to raise issues like, oh, I don't think that that was really great how that person treated this woman. They were really toxic towards her in a way that I thought was unprofessional and let me raise it to one of the managers and let me start raising all these small issues. But nothing was being done. These things would continue to happen. And it got to a point where I was like, you just see it happening and it's getting worse and all of a sudden you see, these people have been at this place for seven years and they're not making progress. All of the women who were junior partners when I was at my firm are no longer there. None of them got promoted to the general partner track and none of them, well, I guess they did, but they're all gone now. So it's not, how can this be a meritocratic environment where women have an equal shot at being successful if none of them stay in the system?

background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: I think a lot of women are afraid to speak up the way you do, which is I think why you were so brave. So can you talk about what, when you got to this decision to actually bring this into the public eye, to actually bring this to court where you knew that you would, you were really exposing yourself and your family.

ground_truth: I was afraid to speak up for a long time. I would be happy to bring up in private situations to a person that I trusted, like, oh, I don't think this is the right thing, but I wouldn't call it out in a meeting because you would get, you would be seen as that annoying person who keeps bringing up these women issues. At least that's what I was worried about. So it took a long time. It took seeing that it was happening to other women. It took hearing that there was a problem that another woman had raised with harassment that wasn't being addressed. She had gone to every managing partner with a letter detailing what had happened to her. And her response was, you should feel flattered. And to me, they had promised me that they were going to take care of this problem. And there was just, it was clear that they weren't willing to address it head on.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: So, in 2012, you brought Kleiner Perkins to court. Very well publicized. I know that many of us watched it and with great admiration because of your bravery. Ultimately, they ruled against you. Why? What went wrong?

ground_truth: What would you have done differently? I think the one thing that would have helped me is if I had had more cash to invest in it. If I'd had $10 million to hire the teams of lawyers, to hire the nasty PR firm, to hire the groups of people that were needed to influence the public opinion, to influence the jury, to influence how we selected the jury. At the end, everybody who said that they believe that tech was biased was kicked out of the jury pool. So you end up with this very odd mix of people who don't think tech is unfair. And so when they hear the stories, they don't believe it. I think the legal system is not a great mechanism for resolving disputes, because it shares some of the fundamental systematic issues that these industries face around whether women are believed, how women are perceived, whether you can manipulate a stereotype to try to fit a story into it. It wasn't a great experience either. I talked to several women before I litigated, and these were women who sued investment banks. And they're just like, don't do it. We don't regret doing it, and we're very grateful for the experience and the opportunity to create change within our organizations, but it is so hard. It is just. You would not wish it on your worst enemy. It is brutal. But once you get through it, you realize you connect with so many people. There are so many people who just stop me in the street to say thank you, who have felt the courage to share their own stories, whether it's just with a colleague or with their kids or with their friends, where people are now understanding that this is going on everywhere. I mean, I'm at a general conference, not a tech conference in Massachusetts, not in California, because people are interested in hearing these stories, and they have their own experiences.

ground_truth: That's a good question. I look back, I don't think I understood the magnitude of how hard it was going to be. I didn't understand that I would have to stay and go to work every day after having filed suit. And I didn't understand how many people would turn on me and the ways that they would do it. I understood it conceptually, but I didn't understand emotionally how hard that would be. So if you could rewind, would you do it all again? Yes. So I come out of it the same way that everybody else does. Yes. I have heard so many stories. I've connected with so many people. I get to meet you. I mean, it's been a very wonderful experience from the other side where people, they really connect because we've all had these experiences. We've been afraid to talk about them. And now there's a kind of framework for thinking. Thinking about it. People are doing, sharing research. Just down the street, Babson College has done some great research. Harvard Business School has done some great research to show that all of these little things and these experiences that we're having, they're real. It's not in our imagination. It's not us being sensitive. It's not us looking for problems that don't exist. This is a very real problem. And having people talk about it and tell their stories, even if it's just to one or two other people is very powerful. Somebody stopped me on the street. I guess about three weeks ago, it was a white man, young, and, you know, he wanted to say thank you. And I was very curious. He said, I want to thank you because I know what you're doing for people. And even though it doesn't affect me, I have a coworker who was sexually harassed. And she didn't do anything about it because the system is so bad. But because you've gone out to tell, you know, tell what happened to you, that's helping everyone. So thank you. Thank you for that. So the stories are working. Like, people are understanding it. And you don't have to go out and sue and take on the risk and the experience that I had. But if you can help people understand, if you can speak up for other people who aren't comfortable speaking up for themselves, it makes a difference. I think people sharing their stories with me helped fuel me through the process. It was hard. But, you know, I would get emails from people who would share their stories about the experiences they had and how grateful they were that somebody was finally speaking up.

Even if you don't feel that way, even if it feels very lonely, you are not alone. And that was a really powerful message I got.

background.text: How important is finding a mentor or a sponsor within the company? Somebody, did you feel like you had somebody you could go speak to?

ground_truth: That's a good question. I had somebody who was my mentor, but he didn't look like me. He didn't experience the things I had experienced. So it was very difficult to get the same opportunities. I think it's important, but it's hard. So yes, everybody should have a sponsor, somebody who's pushing them through and making sure they get the opportunities and telling them that they should get promoted and helping get the raise. Everybody else is, and you shouldn't feel like there's somebody who's favoring you because everybody is getting favored. But it's not always possible.
